8VC3Zffo2KpM.text: To solve this, let's consider what we know about matrices and their dimensions

L8bn8v4yGZUb.text: @Matrix transpose@ is an operator which can be applied to a matrix

4mQMMXmchfoe.text: If we have a matrix @Matrix A@ of dimension M x N, then its transpose is denoted as @Matrix A^t@ and has a dimension of N x M

oUjcnkAMpLGn.text: Now, let's look at the expression @\hat{u}^t \hat{u}@

aqw8aq2RdsQa.text: Here, @\hat{u}@ is likely a column vector with k rows

C5fruMVxjtwm.text: In that case, @\hat{u}^t @ is a 1 x k matrix, where the superscript 't' denotes the transpose operation

t2rQ4cRum5Aw.text: Now that we have @\hat{u}^t @ as a 1 x k matrix, when we multiply it with @\hat{u}@, we get a scalar value, because the resulting product has dimensions 1 x k (1 row, k columns) * k x 1 (k rows, 1 column) = 1 x 1

dMvJeaznLp7v.text: Thus, applying the rules of matrix multiplication and dimensions, we have @\hat{u}^t \hat{u}@ dimension as @1 x 1@
